name: Phishing & Social Engineering
description: Phishing, social engineering, disinformation, and human-targeted deception.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list pushed phishing and social engineering research beyond the classic email inbox. In USENIX 2018, "Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa" showed that voice assistants could be tricked into routing users to imposter "skills" through homophone confusion, while "End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks" (USENIX 2018) documented how weak email authentication still let spoofed spear-phishing slip past major providers. Together they framed the core tension of the area: technical channels keep changing, but the human at the end remains the target.

Around 2019-2020 the field shifted toward large-scale measurement and understanding why deception works. "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" (USENIX 2019) and "High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise" (USENIX 2019) moved detection inside the enterprise, where attacks come from already-compromised trusted accounts, while "Cognitive Triaging of Phishing Attacks" (USENIX 2019) and "Users Really Do Answer Telephone Scams" (USENIX 2019) brought psychology and human factors to the foreground. The two 2020 measurement studies, "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime," traced the full lifecycle of phishing campaigns and the real-world effectiveness (and gaps) of anti-phishing blacklists, establishing that the defensive ecosystem leaks badly.

The early 2020s brought a strong turn to visual and content-based detection, plus the cat-and-mouse of evasion. "Phishpedia" (USENIX 2021) pioneered deep-learning reference-based detection that visually matches a suspect page to known brands, a thread continued by "Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics" (USENIX 2022), "Knowledge Expansion and Counterfactual Interaction" (USENIX 2023), and the reference-list-free "Less Defined Knowledge and More True Alarms" (USENIX 2024). Meanwhile attackers adapted: "PhishPrint" (USENIX 2021) evaded detection crawlers and "PhishDecloaker" (USENIX 2024) tackled CAPTCHA-cloaked sites. A parallel line attacked the telephone channel, with "SnorCall," "UCBlocker," and "Combating Robocalls with Phone Virtual Assistant Mediated Interaction" (all USENIX 2023).

Most recently the field has pivoted to generative AI on both sides. "KnowPhish" (USENIX 2024) folds large language models and multimodal knowledge graphs into phishing detection, while "DeepPhish" (USENIX 2022) and especially "Malicious LLM-Based Conversational AI Makes Users Reveal Personal Information" (USENIX 2025) show AI itself becoming the social-engineering weapon. The area now spans automated brand-spoofing detection, telephone and robocall defense, and a growing concern that conversational AI can manipulate humans directly, returning to that original lesson that the person, not the protocol, is the soft target.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection is grounded in telephone fraud. "Towards Measuring the Effectiveness of Telephony Blacklists" (NDSS 2018) asked a defender's question — do blacklists actually stop scam calls? — and the theme carried into the early 2020s with studies of automated calling and premium-rate abuse, including "Are You Going to Answer That? Measuring User Responses to Anti-Robocall Application Indicators" (NDSS 2020) and "Understanding and Detecting International Revenue Share Fraud" (NDSS 2021). These papers share a measurement mindset: characterize the abuse channel, then test whether existing defenses work.

Around 2020 the center of gravity moved to social platforms and the web, where deception is baked into the interface itself. "Deceptive Previews: A Study of the Link Preview Trustworthiness in Social Platforms" (NDSS 2020) and "To Err.Is Human: Characterizing the Threat of Unintended URLs in Social Media" (NDSS 2021) showed that the machinery meant to make sharing friendly — auto-generated previews, auto-linked text — can itself be weaponized, while "Into the Deep Web: Understanding E-commerce Fraud from Autonomous Chat with Cybercriminals" (NDSS 2020) probed the criminal supply side directly.

By 2023 the field broadened in two directions at once: money and truth. Cryptocurrency became the dominant lure, headlined by the heavily cited "Double and Nothing: Understanding and Detecting Cryptocurrency Giveaway Scams" (NDSS 2023) and later "Like, Comment, Get Scammed: Characterizing Comment Scams on Media Platforms" (NDSS 2024) and "The Kids Are All Right: Investigating the Susceptibility of Teens and Adults to YouTube Giveaway Scams" (NDSS 2025), which brought the human-susceptibility angle to the front. In parallel, "Tactics, Threats & Targets: Modeling Disinformation and its Mitigation" (NDSS 2023) and "Folk Models of Misinformation on Social Media" (NDSS 2023) expanded the area beyond fraud to disinformation and how ordinary users reason about it. Infrastructure-level deception stayed in view too, with "BreakSPF" (NDSS 2024) and "Misdirection of Trust: Demystifying the Abuse of Dedicated URL Shortening Service" (NDSS 2025) showing how trusted email and URL plumbing gets subverted, and "Ctrl+Alt+Deceive: Quantifying User Exposure to Online Scams" (NDSS 2025) measuring how much of this actually reaches people.

The most recent work reflects two forces reshaping the area: blockchain targets and large language models. Ethereum-specific studies like "Dissecting Payload-based Transaction Phishing on Ethereum" (NDSS 2025), "Phishing in Wonderland: Evaluating Learning-Based Ethereum Phishing Transaction Detection and Pitfalls" (NDSS 2026), and "CtPhishCapture: Uncovering Credential-Theft-Based Phishing Scams Targeting Cryptocurrency Wallets" (NDSS 2026) treat the crypto ecosystem as its own phishing frontier. At the same time, defenses are turning to machine learning and confronting AI-generated attacks head-on: "Paladin: Defending LLM-enabled Phishing Emails with a New Trigger-Tag Paradigm" (NDSS 2026) tackles phishing written by LLMs, while "LOKI: Proactively Discovering Online Scam Websites by Mining Toxic Search Queries" and "PhishLang: A Real-Time, Fully Client-Side Phishing Detection Framework Using MobileBERT" (both NDSS 2026) push detection toward proactive discovery and lightweight, on-device transformer models. The arc runs from measuring whether phone blacklists work to shipping real-time neural phishing detectors in the browser — and to defending against deception that machines now generate.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this set treats phishing and social engineering as a measurement and detection problem, cataloguing the machinery scammers use and building automated filters against it. "Surveylance: Automatically Detecting Online Survey Scams" (S&P 2018) and "A Machine Learning Approach to Prevent Malicious Calls over Telephony Networks" (S&P 2018) both aim classifiers at specific fraud channels, while "PhishFarm: A Scalable Framework for Measuring the Effectiveness of Evasion Techniques against Browser Phishing Blacklists" (S&P 2019) shifts the lens to the defenders' blind spots, showing how attackers dodge the blacklists meant to stop them. "CrawlPhish: Large-scale Analysis of Client-side Cloaking Techniques in Phishing" (S&P 2021) deepens that thread, systematically dissecting the cloaking tricks phishing kits use to hide from crawlers.

A second phase widens the definition of the threat well beyond the classic fake-login page. The COVID era brought "A First Look at Zoombombing" (S&P 2021) and a wave of platform-abuse and influence studies: "TrollMagnifier: Detecting State-Sponsored Troll Accounts on Reddit" (S&P 2022) and "Lambretta: Learning to Rank for Twitter Soft Moderation" (S&P 2023) push into disinformation and content moderation, while "Analyzing Ground-Truth Data of Mobile Gambling Scams" (S&P 2022) and "Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale" (S&P 2023) show the field chasing scams into new economic niches. Crucially, the community also turned from the attacker to the target: "Phishing in Organizations: Findings from a Large-Scale and Long-Term Study" (S&P 2022) ran a real long-term experiment inside a company, and "Design and Evaluation of Inclusive Email Security Indicators for People with Visual Impairments" (S&P 2023) foregrounded users who standard defenses ignore.

The arrival of large language models marks the sharpest recent shift, cutting in both directions. "From Chatbots to Phishbots?: Phishing Scam Generation in Commercial Large Language Models" (S&P 2024) shows LLMs can mass-produce convincing lures, while "Moderating New Waves of Online Hate with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models" (S&P 2024) turns the same models into moderators. Alongside this, the field kept mapping concrete attack infrastructure and human harms: "On SMS Phishing Tactics and Infrastructure" (S&P 2024), "Conning the Crypto Conman: End-to-End Analysis of Cryptocurrency-based Technical Support Scams" (S&P 2024), "No Easy Way Out: the Effectiveness of Deplatforming an Extremist Forum" (S&P 2024), and "Children, Parents, and Misinformation on Social Media" (S&P 2024) span telephony, crypto fraud, extremism, and family dynamics. A notable finding from this period is that interventions are harder than they look — "Understanding the Efficacy of Phishing Training in Practice" (S&P 2025) empirically questions whether standard enterprise training and simulated-phishing actually help.

The most recent work concentrates on warnings, telephony trust, and previously overlooked victims. Human-factors studies such as "Restricting the Link: Effects of Focused Attention and Time Delay on Phishing Warning Effectiveness" (S&P 2025) and "(Blind) Users Really Do Heed Aural Telephone Scam Warnings" (S&P 2025) test what actually changes user behavior, and the 2026 papers push this further: "From 'Be Careful' to 'Here's Why': Investigating User Reasoning with Context-Specific SMS Scam Warnings" (S&P 2026) argues that explaining the why beats generic caution. On the infrastructure side, "STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness" (S&P 2026) exposes weaknesses in the caller-ID authentication meant to curb robocalls, "Lost in Translation: Text Message Spoofing via Email" (S&P 2026) reveals a fresh spoofing vector, and "International Students and Scams: At Risk Abroad" (S&P 2026) centers a specific vulnerable population. Together the latest work signals a field that has largely stopped treating detection as the whole game and now asks how to warn, authenticate, and protect the people most exposed.

ccs.narrative:
Phishing research at CCS has tracked the evolution of deceptive attacks from credential-harvesting web pages to blockchain transaction fraud. The 2018 cohort examined mobile and password-reuse dimensions: Phishing Attacks on Modern Android (CCS 2018) showed that Android's Instant Apps and password managers could be exploited to launch convincing in-app phishing, while "What was that site doing with my Facebook password?": Designing Password-Reuse Notifications (CCS 2018) addressed the usability gap in warning users about cross-site credential exposure.

Visual similarity became the dominant detection paradigm in 2020: VisualPhishNet: Zero-Day Phishing Website Detection by Visual Similarity (CCS 2020) learned visual embeddings of legitimate brand pages to detect zero-day phishing without URL signatures. Catching Transparent Phish: Analyzing and Detecting MITM Phishing Toolkits (CCS 2021) characterized a newer threat class—reverse-proxy toolkits like Modlishka that transparently relay the real site while harvesting credentials.

Blockchain-specific phishing emerged as a major new category. TxPhishScope: Towards Detecting and Understanding Transaction-based Phishing on Ethereum (CCS 2023) analyzed the on-chain transaction patterns that distinguish phishing drainer contracts from legitimate DeFi interactions. Phishing URL Detection: A Network-based Approach Robust to Evasion (CCS 2022) revisited URL-based detection with network-layer features that resist evasion, and Clues in Tweets: Twitter-Guided Discovery and Analysis of SMS Spam (CCS 2022) used social media signals to discover emerging SMS phishing campaigns.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats phishing and social engineering as a measurement and channel problem. Around 2018, researchers mapped how attacks arrive: email spoofing that providers still fail to block ("End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks," USENIX 2018), novel surfaces like voice assistants ("Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa," USENIX 2018) and Android UI ("Phishing Attacks on Modern Android," CCS 2018), and the telephony channel, where blacklists were tested ("Towards Measuring the Effectiveness of Telephony Blacklists," NDSS 2018) and ML was applied to spam calls ("A Machine Learning Approach to Prevent Malicious Calls over Telephony Networks," S&P 2018). A parallel thread began studying the human and organizational side, from why people fall for scams ("Users Really Do Answer Telephone Scams," USENIX 2019) to detecting attacks that abuse trusted internal accounts ("Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale," USENIX 2019) and business email compromise ("High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise," USENIX 2019).

The turn of the decade brought two big shifts. First, detection moved from URLs and blacklists to visual and reference-based methods that recognize a spoofed brand by how a page looks: "VisualPhishNet" (CCS 2020) flagged zero-day sites by visual similarity, and "Phishpedia" (USENIX 2021) plus "Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics" (USENIX 2022) made identification both deep-learning-driven and explainable. Second, a strong measurement-of-the-defense-ecosystem program emerged, tracking the full lifecycle and the arms race against crawlers: "Sunrise to Sunset" (USENIX 2020) and "PhishTime" (USENIX 2020) quantified how long attacks live and how quickly blacklists react, while "PhishFarm" (S&P 2019) and "PhishPrint" (USENIX 2021) showed attackers evading detectors, and "Catching Transparent Phish" (CCS 2021) exposed real-time MITM phishing toolkits that defeat two-factor authentication.

By the early 2020s the field broadened beyond classic credential phishing into the wider deception landscape: state-sponsored trolls and disinformation ("TrollMagnifier," S&P 2022), deepfake social-media profiles ("DeepPhish," USENIX 2022), SMS spam ("Clues in Tweets," CCS 2022), e-commerce fraud ("Beyond Phish," S&P 2023), and a wave of cryptocurrency scams, from giveaway fraud ("Double and Nothing," NDSS 2023) to on-chain transaction phishing ("TxPhishScope," CCS 2023). Large controlled studies also matured our understanding of what actually works, notably "Phishing in Organizations" (S&P 2022), a long-term embedded-training experiment.

The most recent work is defined by large language models cutting both ways and by a return to hard channel-level problems. LLMs now power detection ("KnowPhish," USENIX 2024, and reference-free detection in "Less Defined Knowledge and More True Alarms," USENIX 2024) and lightweight client-side systems ("PhishLang," NDSS 2026), but they also generate attacks at scale ("From Chatbots to Phishbots?," S&P 2024), prompting LLM-specific defenses like "Paladin" (NDSS 2026). The 2026 papers show the frontier splitting into crypto-wallet credential theft ("CtPhishCapture," NDSS 2026) and Ethereum detection pitfalls ("Phishing in Wonderland," NDSS 2026), proactive scam discovery ("LOKI," NDSS 2026), social-bot campaigns ("TBTrackerX," NDSS 2026), and a renewed focus on the telephone and SMS ecosystem and its victims — dissecting STIR/SHAKEN's weaknesses ("STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness," S&P 2026), text-message spoofing via email ("Lost in Translation," S&P 2026), scam-warning design ("From 'Be Careful' to 'Here's Why'," S&P 2026), and understudied victims ("International Students and Scams," S&P 2026).
